# Job 19 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

Matthew Henry calls this “Job’s answer to Bildad’s discourse.” He notes that although Job's spirit was heated, he let Bildad finish before answering fairly. The chapter divides into: (1) complaint of unkind usage by friends (vv. 2–7), (2) complaint that God is the author of his affliction (vv. 8–12), (3) estrangement of relations and friends (vv. 13–22), (4) a solemn confession of faith (vv. 23–27), and (5) a caution to his friends (vv. 28–29).
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

David Guzik (Enduring Word) calls this “a turning point” — Job reaches a new low in rejection and a new high in confidence in God. Constable (StudyLight excerpt) notes Job uses seven figures to describe himself: an animal trapped, a criminal in court, a traveler fenced in, a king dethroned, a structure destroyed, a tree uprooted, and a city besieged.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-19/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-19.html

---

## Verses 1–6: Job Complains That His Friends Have Not Understood Him

### v. 1 — “Then Job answered:”

Gill notes Job heard Bildad out without interruption, then rose in his own defence.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/19.htm

### v. 2 — “How long will you torment me and crush me with your words?”

**Ellicott** observes Job begins as Bildad himself had begun in both his speeches (“How long?”). Bildad's last speech had been so offensive and unfeeling that Job may well ask this. Bildad had infused “personal malice into his charges.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/19.htm

**Gill** explains “vex my soul” is the worst kind of vexation — not only Job's bones were vexed (by disease) but now his soul by his friends. “Break me in pieces with words” refers not to his body but his spirit; Job was “smitten with the tongues of men” as Jeremiah was, beaten as with a pestle in a mortar.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/19.htm

**Enduring Word** cites Spurgeon: “They struck at him with their hard words, as if they were breaking stones on the roadside. We ought to be very careful what we say to those who are suffering affliction and trial.” D.L. Moody adds: “The church has become very jealous about men being unsound in the faith… But he may be ever so unsound in love, and they don’t say anything.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-19/

### v. 3 — “Ten times now you have reproached me; you shamelessly mistreat me.”

**Gill** says “ten times” does not denote an exact count but “many times” — the phrase is used this way elsewhere (Genesis 31:7). His friends’ lack of shame in reproaching him was an argument of great hardness.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/19.htm

**Matthew Henry**: “Five times they had spoken, and every speech was a double reproach.” He notes the friends “were not ashamed of what they did” — of “hard-heartedness, so ill becoming men… uncharitableness, so ill becoming good men… deceitfulness, so ill becoming friends.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

### v. 4 — “Even if I have truly gone astray, my error concerns me alone.”

**Gill** says this is a concession for argument’s sake, not an acknowledgement. Job means: even if he has erred, he alone is answerable — the friends don't suffer from it. Gill gives an alternative: “let it remain with me” — i.e., “I will hold it fast; it shall remain with me as a principle never to be departed from.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/19.htm

**Matthew Henry**: “Men’s errors are the more excusable if they keep them to themselves, and do not disturb others with them.” He also adds: “If I be in an error, it is I that must smart for it… you need not add to my misery by your reproaches.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

### v. 5 — “If indeed you would exalt yourselves above me and use my disgrace against me…”

**Gill**: “Look and talk big, set up themselves for great folk, and resolve to run him down” — to “magnify” what they called an error and “set it out in the worst light they could.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/19.htm

**Matthew Henry**: “It is a mean thing, it is a base thing, thus to trample upon those that are down.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

### v. 6 — “…understand that it is God who has wronged me and drawn His net around me.”

**Ellicott**: Bildad had spoken much about the wicked being snared by his own sin. Job now answers: It is God who has taken him in His net, not his own sin.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/19.htm

**Enduring Word**: “If God had sent or allowed this calamity in Job’s life, it could be said that God had wronged Job because the calamity was not a just penalty for some sin in Job.” Guzik adds: “In a sense the Accuser was acting as the hand of God, for he had said to God, ‘But stretch out your hand and strike his flesh’ (2:5). And God had replied, ‘Very well, then, he is in your hands’ (2:6). So Job was not totally wrong when he said, ‘The hand of God has struck me’ (19:21).” (Citing Smick)
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-19/

**Gill**: The word “overthrown” (or “perverted”) means God has brought him into “cross, crooked, and afflictive dispensations.” The “net” is God’s net of affliction, which He “has made, ordained, and makes use of… which he lays for his people, and takes them in, and draws them to himself.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/19.htm

---

## Verses 7–12: Job Describes How God Has Attacked Him

### v. 7 — “Though I cry out, ‘Violence!’ I get no response; though I call for help, there is no justice.”

**Gill**: Job cries out concerning “violence” or injury done him by the Sabeans and Chaldeans, and by Satan upon his health. He cried to God as in an open court, but was not heard — no relief, no redress, no knowledge of reasons.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/19.htm

**Enduring Word**: “Job was accustomed to finding comfort and some sense of an answer from God in his previous trials. Yet now when he cried out to heaven, he heard no reply.” Trapp is cited: “Nothing is more natural and usual than for men in misery to cry out for help. Job’s great grief was, that neither God nor man would regard his moans.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-19/

### v. 8 — “He has blocked my way so I cannot pass; He has veiled my paths with darkness.”

**Gill**: A metaphor from a traveller who finds his way fenced up and cannot pass. This may refer not only to Job’s walk in this world but to “his way to God, either to the throne of his grace, or the tribunal of his justice.” When God hides His face, the way seems fenced up. Darkness in his paths is like “a traveller in a very dark night, that cannot see his way, and knows not what step to take next.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/19.htm

### v. 9 — “He has stripped me of my honor and removed the crown from my head.”

**Gill**: Not spiritual glory (the robe of Christ’s righteousness) but civil glory — wealth, children, fine clothes, stately palace. “These things are very properly and significantly expressed by clothes a man is stripped of, because they are outward things, as garments are.” Gill explicitly rejects the idea that Job was a king (Jobab of Edom); he “wore a better diadem… even his righteousness, justice, and integrity” (Job 29:14).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/19.htm

**Matthew Henry**: “See the vanity of worldly glory: it is what we may be soon stripped of; and, whatever strips us, we must see and own God’s hand in it.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

### v. 10 — “He tears me down on every side until I am gone; He uproots my hope like a tree.”

**Gill**: The metaphor may be of a building demolished or a tree dug about on all sides and its roots cut off. The hope removed is “not his hope of salvation, of the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal life, which was strong and firm” but his “hope of a restoration to outward happiness.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/19.htm

**Matthew Henry** adds a pastoral note: “Hope in this life is a perishing thing, but the hope of good men, when it is cut off from this world, is but removed like a tree, transplanted from this nursery to the garden of the Lord.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

### v. 11 — “His anger burns against me, and He counts me among His enemies.”

**Matthew Henry**: “What is the fire of hell but the wrath of God? Seared consciences will feel it hereafter, but do not fear it now. Enlightened consciences fear it now, but shall not feel it hereafter.” He notes it is “a gross mistake, but a very common one, to think that whom God afflicts he treats as his enemies; whereas… as many as he loves he rebukes and chastens; it is the discipline of his sons.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

**Enduring Word**: “Though Job could not comprehend it (nor be expected to), God still held him in special favor and care.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-19/

### v. 12 — “His troops advance together; they construct a ramp against me and encamp around my tent.”

**Enduring Word** notes the reverse progression of siege warfare in vv. 8–12: captivity → dethronement → wall torn down → uprooted tree → siege → surrounded. Smick is cited: “Reverse this order and you have a step-by-step description of what happened in siege warfare… God’s troops laid siege as if Job were a fortified city; but, alas, he was only a tent.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-19/

**Matthew Henry**: “It did not so much trouble him that his miseries came upon him in troops as that they were God’s troops, in whom it seemed as if God fought against him.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

---

## Verses 13–20: The Bitter Results of God’s Attack — Social Isolation

### v. 13 — “He has removed my brothers from me; my acquaintances have abandoned me.”

**Ellicott** notes the Psalmist apparently copied this in Psalm 88:8: “It is not easy to read these sad complaints of Job without seeing how fitly they apply to the sorrows of the Man of sorrows.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/19.htm

**Matthew Henry**: “As it was their sin God was not the author of it; it is Satan that alienates men’s minds from their brethren in affliction. But, as it was Job’s trouble, God ordered it for the completing of his trial.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

### vv. 14–16 — Kinsmen, friends, guests, maidservants, and servants all abandon Job.

**Peake’s Commentary** (StudyLight excerpt): In v. 17 it is better to read “mother’s” (body) than “womb.” Job’s children were all dead, unless he had others by concubines (though Job 31:1 is against this).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-19.html

### v. 17 — “My breath is repulsive to my wife, and I am loathsome to my own family.”

**Ellicott** renders: “and so is my affection or kindness (see Psalm 77:10) to the children of my mother’s womb, i.e., my brethren.” Others render: “I am become offensive to them.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/19.htm

**Enduring Word** notes that “the children of my own body” must be either grandchildren, symbolically Job’s children, or possibly younger children who escaped the catastrophe (so Adam Clarke). Smick adds: “In any society nothing hurts more than rejection by one’s family and friends, but what could be worse in a patriarchal society than to have children ridicule the patriarch?”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-19/

**Matthew Henry** on the wife: “the devil spared her to him, not only to be his tempter, but to be his tormentor.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

**Spurgeon** (CCEL, cited in Enduring Word summary): Job had lost his wife “for all practical purposes, for she had not acted like a wife to him in his time of trial.”
— https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons50/sermons50.xlv.html

### v. 18 — “Even little boys scorn me; when I appear, they deride me.”

**Matthew Henry**: “the children of his own servants, who were his servants by birth, despised him… though he arose in civility to speak friendly to them, or with authority to check them, they let him know that they neither feared him nor loved him.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

### v. 19 — “All my best friends despise me, and those I love have turned against me.”

**Ellicott**: “My inward friends — that is, my intimate friends: the men of my counsel who are familiar with my secret affairs.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/19.htm

**Matthew Henry**: “Those whom he loved… not only turned from him, but were turned against him, and did all they could to make him odious, so to justify themselves in being so strange to him.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

### v. 20 — “My skin and flesh cling to my bones; I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.”

**Ellicott**: “My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh in one indistinguishable mass, and I have escaped with the skin of my teeth, because the teeth have no skin, or, as others explain, because the teeth have fallen out. This expression… has passed into a proverb expressive of a very narrow escape — a meaning which can only by inference be obtained from this place in Job.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/19.htm

**Enduring Word** cites Spurgeon: “There is no skin upon the teeth, or scarcely any, and, therefore, Job means that there was next to nothing of him left, like the skin of his teeth.” Smick adds: “The KJV made a literal translation of it and thereby created an idiom in the English language for a narrow escape.” Trapp suggests: “All I have left me whole is the skin of my teeth; that is, of my gums… the rest of my body is all over of a scab.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-19/

**Peake’s Commentary** (StudyLight excerpt): The exact meaning of “the skin of my teeth” is not certain.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-19.html

---

## Verses 21–22: Job Pleads for Pity

### v. 21 — “Have pity on me, my friends, have pity, for the hand of God has struck me.”

**Matthew Henry**: “This he begs in the most moving melting language that could be, enough (one would think) to break a heart of stone.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

**Spurgeon** (CCEL): “This strong man — this most patient man — this perfect and upright man before God has to ask for sympathy! Do you wonder that it was so? He, who was far greater than Job, ran back thrice to His sleeping disciples… ‘What? Could you not watch with Me one hour?’”
— https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons50/sermons50.xlv.html

### v. 22 — “Why do you persecute me as God does? Will you never get enough of my flesh?”

**Matthew Henry**: “If they did delight in his calamity, let them be satisfied with his flesh, which was wasted and gone, but let them not, as if that were too little, wound his spirit, and ruin his good name.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

---

## Verses 23–27: Job’s Triumphant Proclamation of Faith

### vv. 23–24 — “I wish that my words were recorded and inscribed in a book, by an iron stylus on lead, or chiseled in stone forever.”

**Ellicott**: Some take this as referring to the words he is about to utter; others interpret it generally. Ellicott favors the view that it is especially the words of vv. 25–27 that Job desires recorded. “Oh that they were printed — this points us to primitive time, when writing materials and the use of writing involved more or less of engraving, as, for instance, in later times was the case with tablets of wax.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/19.htm

**Enduring Word**: “Job seemed to have no sense that his own personal tragedy and drama would indeed be written and inscribed in a book and be so for the benefit of countless others through succeeding generations. His words and life were indeed written with an iron pen and lead, forever!”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-19/

### v. 25 — “But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth.”

This is the most commented-upon verse in the chapter. Multiple interpretive questions arise:

#### The meaning of “Redeemer” (Hebrew *goel*)

**Ellicott**: “This goel was the name given to the next of kin whose duty it was to redeem, ransom, or avenge one who had fallen into debt or bondage, or had been slain in a family feud. In Ruth, for instance, the goel is he who has to marry the widow of his relative.” Job is assured God will take on this role for him — to avenge, be surety, vindicate. “He states most emphatically that he himself knows that this Goel liveth. ‘And I, even I know; as for me, I know that my Vindicator is living.’”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/19.htm

**Enduring Word** (Morgan): “The ‘Goel’ stood for another to defend his cause, to avenge wrongs done to him, and so to acquit him of all charges laid against him.” Lawson is cited: “A redeemer was a vindicator of one unjustly wronged. He was a defender of the oppressed. A champion of the suffering. An advocate of one unjustly accused.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-19/

**Dummelow** (StudyLight excerpt): “Redeemer — Heb. Go’el… The Go’el was the next of kin whose duty it was to prevent land being sold out of the clan (Leviticus 25:25), and to avenge murder… Driver points out that the word means here the opposite to the Christian idea, viz. a deliverer, not from sin, but from affliction and wrong not due to sin. The best rendering here is ‘Vindicator.’” Dummelow adds: “The vindicator is God Himself, who is now his persecutor, and Job anticipates neither deliverance from death nor a resurrection of the body after death… only… his shade will wake from its semi-conscious stupor to see God standing over his grave and declaring his innocence.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/job-19.html

**Spurgeon** (CCEL) expands the *goel* to three senses: (1) Kinsman — Christ is our near kinsman by taking on human nature; (2) Vindicator — Christ will clear our name; (3) Redeemer — Christ redeems by price (His sacrifice) and by power (His Spirit renewing us). “There are two redemptions — redemption by price and redemption by power, and both of these Christ hath wrought for us.”
— https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons50/sermons50.xlv.html

#### “He shall stand at the last upon the earth” (or “upon the dust”)

**Ellicott**: “Upon the earth is literally, upon dust; the word is thus used in Job 41:33. This usage… is strongly against the rendering some have preferred: over the dust, or over my dust.” He renders: “He shall stand last upon earth” — i.e., after all others have passed away.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/19.htm

**BibleHub footnotes**: The alternative reading is “on my grave.”
— https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/job/19.htm

**Pulpit Commentary Homiletics** (BibleHub): “God is here viewed as he who will outlive all, especially in contrast to Job, now sinking into death. He will rise, stand up for Job’s defence and deliverance, on the dust in which he shall soon be laid.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/19.htm

#### Who is the Redeemer — God Himself, or a separate Person?

**Enduring Word** (Andersen): “Verses 25-27 are so tightly knit that there should be no doubt that the Redeemer is God.” Also: “Job cannot understand why God is now acting so completely out of character… He boldly claims God as his nearest relative.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-19/

**Gill** sees Christ here directly: “And if the places where God is called Goel in the Old Testament be examined, it will be found that either all or most of them may be, and some of them must be, understood of God the Son, or of Christ, as Genesis 48:16; Isaiah 59:20.” (Citing Poole)
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/19.htm

**Spurgeon** also sees Christ: “He throws his faith forward to some tremendous era… a Goel, a Kinsman, an Avenger who will stand up for him.” But Spurgeon allows that “Job, himself, may not have known the full meaning of all that he said.”
— https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons50/sermons50.xlv.html

**John Piper** (Desiring God, search excerpt): “I know that my Redeemer lives… I think from our vantage point, it’s Christ, ultimately, who redeemed him, but he knew that God would be a Redeemer for him… I think that it’s an affirmation of the resurrection of his own body in the presence of his Redeemer.”
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/holding-on-to-your-faith-in-the-midst-of-suffering-job-part-2

### v. 26 — “Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God.”

This is the most textually and theologically debated verse in the chapter.

#### Translation debate: “in my flesh” vs. “without my flesh” vs. “from my flesh”

**Ellicott**: “The words ‘in my flesh’ may mean from my flesh, or, without my flesh. Taken in the former sense and applied to the future, it is hard not to recognise in them, at the least, some dim conception of a resurrection.” Ellicott takes a mediating position: Job’s words don't necessarily teach bodily resurrection directly, but they “express the firm conviction of that faith of which the resurrection is the only natural justification.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/19.htm

**John Piper** (Desiring God): “There’s some translation question about whether you translate ‘from my flesh,’ meaning ‘apart from my flesh,’ I will see God, or ‘out of my flesh I will see God’ because I’ll be raised with new flesh. I’m inclined to think that’s probably what it means.”
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/holding-on-to-your-faith-in-the-midst-of-suffering-job-part-2

**Peake’s Commentary** (StudyLight excerpt): “The second line may bear quite opposite meanings. The word translated ‘from’ may mean ‘without’ or it may mean ‘in’… Probably we should translate ‘without,’ referring the passage to an experience after death. Job expresses his confidence that not only will God appear as his vindicator, but that he will see Him.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-19.html

**Dummelow** (StudyLight excerpt): “It is unfortunate that the rendering ‘Redeemer’ and the traditional reference of the vindicator to Christ, together with the supposition that Job expects a resurrection of the body, have completely disguised the true meaning from most readers.” Dummelow translates: “And after (the loss of) my skin, which has been destroyed (i.e. after my death) this shall be, I shall have vision of God.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/job-19.html

#### The traditional / conservative reading

**Gill** takes a strong resurrection view: Job “expresses his strong faith in his living Redeemer, who should appear on the earth in the latter day, and be his Saviour, and in the resurrection of the dead through him, which he believed he should share in.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/19.htm

**Matthew Henry**: “These were the things he comforted himself with the expectation of, and not a deliverance from his trouble or a revival of his happiness in this world, as some would understand him… It is very plain that he had no expectation at all of his return to a prosperous condition in this world.” Henry insists Job looks for “the redemption of his soul from the power of the grave, and his reception to glory.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

**Enduring Word**: “Though Job expected the destruction of his skin to be completed, at the same time he had the confidence of faith to know that God would not hide Himself forever; that ‘in my flesh I shall see God.’”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-19/

#### A mediating view (immortality, not necessarily bodily resurrection)

**Pulpit Commentary Homiletics** (BibleHub): “Perhaps the best is that which steers between two extremes… It is that Job does not here express the hope of a bodily resurrection after death, but of a contemplation of God in the other world in a spiritually glorified state. It is the hope of immortality, rather than that of resurrection.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/19.htm

### v. 27 — “I will see Him for myself; my eyes will behold Him, and not as a stranger. How my heart yearns within me!”

**Ellicott**: “The words ‘see for myself’ may mean see on my side, i.e., as my Judge and Avenger.” The BSB footnote notes the Hebrew literally reads “my kidneys yearn” — the deepest, tenderest part of the man.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/19.htm

**Matthew Henry**: “Anticipating the fulfillment of all this, no wonder Job could say, ‘How my heart yearns within me!’”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

**Enduring Word** (Clarke): Adam Clarke “described how he felt this remarkable revelation given to Job changed him… after this time no such words [of impatience and irritation] escaped his lips: He bears the rest of his sufferings with great patience and fortitude.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-19/

## Verses 28–29: Job Warns His Accusers

### v. 28 — “If you say, ‘Let us persecute him, since the root of the matter lies with him’…”

**Ellicott** says this verse is “variously understood.” He prefers: “For ye say, What is a persecuted man to Him (why should He persecute any man without cause?), and therefore the root of the matter (i.e., the cause of the afflictions) is, i.e., must be found in me.” The Authorised Version takes the opposite sense — that the root of the matter (true piety) is found in Job.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/19.htm

**Peake’s Commentary** (StudyLight excerpt): “The last two verses bring us back from heaven to earth. They are difficult and probably corrupt.” Peake reads: “If ye say, How will we persecute him, and find the root of the matter in him (i.e. the real cause of his affliction).”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-19.html

### v. 29 — “…then you should fear the sword yourselves, because wrath brings punishment by the sword, so that you may know there is a judgment.”

**Ellicott**: “Job threatens his friends with that condign punishment of which they regarded him as a conspicuous example.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/19.htm

**Enduring Word** (Andersen): “Job’s concluding words, addressed to the friends, sound like a warning that they, too, must face judgment. Unfortunately these verses are largely unintelligible, including verse 27c, which reads ‘my kidneys have ended in my chest.’”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-19/

**Matthew Henry**: Job appeals “from this wrangle at the bar to the judgment of the bench, even to him to whom all judgment is committed, who he knew would right him.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

## Points of Difference Among Protestant Traditions

### Reformed / Presbyterian

**Matthew Henry** (a Presbyterian of the Puritan tradition) reads vv. 25–27 as a clear confession of resurrection hope and sees Christ as the Redeemer. He treats Job’s words as inspired beyond what Job himself fully understood: “We have reason to think that Job was just now under an extraordinary impulse of the blessed Spirit, which raised him above himself.” Henry also stresses God's sovereignty in affliction: “As it was their sin God was not the author of it… But, as it was Job’s trouble, God ordered it for the completing of his trial.” 
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/19.htm

### Baptist

**Gill** (Reformed Baptist, 18th c.) sees Christ explicitly in the *goel* and reads a full bodily resurrection into v. 26. He emphasizes that the “error” in v. 4 is only a concession for argument’s sake.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/19.htm

**Spurgeon** (Reformed Baptist) celebrates the triple sense of *goel* (Kinsman, Vindicator, Redeemer) and applies all three to Christ. His emphasis is pastoral: “Job had lost everything… but he had not lost his Redeemer!” He also stresses the certainty of Job's “I know”: “The winds may rage and the tempests roar, but they cannot shake this rock.”
— https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons50/sermons50.xlv.html

**John Piper** (Reformed Baptist, Desiring God) affirms bodily resurrection in v. 26 and sees Christ as the Redeemer from a New Testament vantage point. He links the passage to the theme of suffering and the sovereignty of God.
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/holding-on-to-your-faith-in-the-midst-of-suffering-job-part-2

### Pentecostal / Charismatic

**David Guzik** (Enduring Word, charismatic evangelical) emphasizes that Job's “flash of faith” in v. 25 is a supernatural breakthrough: “This is another of the brilliant flashes of faith in Job’s otherwise dark and bleak background of crisis and suffering.” Guzik highlights the emotional and experiential dimension — “How my heart yearns within me!” — and points to the parallels with Christ's suffering. He also applies it to present-day suffering: “When we suffer as Job did, we can fix our eyes on the living Redeemer who will one day stand on earth to vindicate us.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-19/

### Anglican

**Ellicott** (Anglican bishop and scholar, 19th c.) takes a more cautious exegetical approach on the resurrection question: “Do Job’s words then teach the doctrine of the resurrection? Possibly not directly, but they express the firm conviction of that faith of which the resurrection is the only natural justification.” Yet Ellicott also sees Christ foreshadowed: “It is not easy to read these sad complaints of Job without seeing how fitly they apply to the sorrows of the Man of sorrows.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/19.htm

## Other Views

### Modern / Critical Scholarship

**Dummelow** (StudyLight excerpt) argues that the traditional Christian reading (identifying the Redeemer as Christ and expecting bodily resurrection) “completely disguised the true meaning from most readers.” The *goel* / Vindicator is “God Himself, who is now his persecutor,” and Job anticipates only a post-mortem vision of God declaring his innocence, not bodily resurrection.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/job-19.html

**Peake’s Commentary** (StudyLight excerpt) similarly notes that the Hebrew text of v. 26 is “badly corrupt” and “all translations are more or less guesses.” Peake concludes that Job’s confidence is that God will appear as his Vindicator and that Job will see Him — but probably “without” the flesh, an experience after death, not a bodily resurrection. Peake also says vv. 28–29 are “difficult and probably corrupt.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-19.html

## Summary of the Central Theological Debate (vv. 25–27)

| Position | Key Advocates | Reading of v. 26 |
|---|---|---|
| Bodily resurrection | Gill, Matthew Henry, Spurgeon, Piper, Guzik | “in my flesh I will see God” |
| Hope of immortality / spiritual vision after death | Pulpit Homiletics, Ellicott (mediating) | “from / without my flesh I will see God” |
| Post-mortem vindication only, no resurrection | Dummelow, Peake | “without my flesh” — vision of God as Vindicator over his grave |

The BSB itself footnotes “in my flesh” with the alternative “or without my flesh,” reflecting this longstanding translation debate.
— https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/job/19.htm
